claim: TXNIP expression is inversely correlated with monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1) in lung cancer.
source: TXNIP mRNA expression is inversely correlated with three critical regulators of proton export that function to increase intracellular pH (Webb et al., 2011): monocarboxylate transporter (MCT) 1 in lung cancer, MCT4 in breast cancer and sodium-hydrogen antiporter 1 (NHE1) in brain cancer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A using TCGA data

claim: TXNIP expression is inversely correlated with monocarboxylate transporter 4 (MCT4) in breast cancer.
source: TXNIP mRNA expression is inversely correlated with three critical regulators of proton export that function to increase intracellular pH (Webb et al., 2011): monocarboxylate transporter (MCT) 1 in lung cancer, MCT4 in breast cancer and sodium-hydrogen antiporter 1 (NHE1) in brain cancer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A using TCGA data

claim: TXNIP expression is inversely correlated with sodium-hydrogen antiporter 1 (NHE1) in brain cancer.
source: TXNIP mRNA expression is inversely correlated with three critical regulators of proton export that function to increase intracellular pH (Webb et al., 2011): monocarboxylate transporter (MCT) 1 in lung cancer, MCT4 in breast cancer and sodium-hydrogen antiporter 1 (NHE1) in brain cancer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A using TCGA data

claim: TXNIP expression positively correlates with an acidosis gene-signature in breast cancer.
source: In contrast, TXNIP expression positively correlated with an acidosis gene-signature in breast cancer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B using METABRIC breast cancer dataset

claim: TXNIP expression is anti-correlated with MCTs and NHE1 in non-transformed tissues.
source: TXNIP expression was also anti-correlated with MCTs and NHE1 in non-transformed tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D), demonstrating that pH-dependent regulation of MondoA activity at the TXNIP is not restricted to cancer cells.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D using GTEx data

claim: pH-dependent regulation of MondoA activity at TXNIP is not restricted to cancer cells.
source: TXNIP expression was also anti-correlated with MCTs and NHE1 in non-transformed tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D), demonstrating that pH-dependent regulation of MondoA activity at the TXNIP is not restricted to cancer cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TXNIP-MCT/NHE1 correlation is observed in both cancer and non-transformed tissues

claim: Intracellular pH per se, rather than a lactic acidosis-dependent signaling event, controls MondoA transcriptional activity.
source: These data suggest that intracellular pH per se, rather than a lactic acidosis-dependent signaling event, controls MondoA transcriptional activity.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation data showing TXNIP expression patterns with pH regulators across different tissue types

claim: HBSS treatment of murine embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) increases TXNIP mRNA expression.
source: HBSS treatment of murine embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) increased TXNIP mRNA and protein expression, and decreased glucose uptake (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A and immunoblotting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: HBSS treatment of murine embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) increases TXNIP protein expression.
source: HBSS treatment of murine embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) increased TXNIP mRNA and protein expression, and decreased glucose uptake (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: HBSS treatment of murine embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) decreases glucose uptake.
source: HBSS treatment of murine embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) increased TXNIP mRNA and protein expression, and decreased glucose uptake (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by glucose uptake assay data shown in Figure 1B

claim: HBSS has minimal pH-buffering capacity and in 5% CO2 has an acidic pH of ~6.5.
source: HBSS has minimal pH-buffering capacity and in 5% CO2 has an acidic pH of ~6.5.
evidence: Statement about the properties of HBSS medium, based on established knowledge of this medium

claim: HBSS is weakly buffered due to a low level of sodium bicarbonate (0.35 g/L).
source: HBSS is weakly buffered due to a low level of sodium bicarbonate (0.35 g/L).
evidence: Statement about the composition of HBSS medium

claim: Supplementing HBSS with sodium bicarbonate to 3.7 g/L raises the pH to 7.5.
source: Supplementing HBSS with sodium bicarbonate to 3.7 g/L raised the pH to 7.5 and prevented TXNIP induction (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Experimental observation of pH change upon sodium bicarbonate supplementation

claim: Supplementing HBSS with sodium bicarbonate to 3.7 g/L prevents TXNIP induction.
source: Supplementing HBSS with sodium bicarbonate to 3.7 g/L raised the pH to 7.5 and prevented TXNIP induction (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 1C and immunoblotting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: Decreasing sodium bicarbonate in DMEM to 0.37 g/L (DMEMAcidic) decreases the pH to ~6.5.
source: Conversely, decreasing sodium bicarbonate in DMEM to 0.37 g/L (DMEMAcidic) decreased the pH to ~6.5 and induced TXNIP expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Experimental observation of pH change upon sodium bicarbonate reduction

claim: Decreasing sodium bicarbonate in DMEM to 0.37 g/L (DMEMAcidic) induces TXNIP expression.
source: Conversely, decreasing sodium bicarbonate in DMEM to 0.37 g/L (DMEMAcidic) decreased the pH to ~6.5 and induced TXNIP expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: Low pH rather than low sodium bicarbonate is primarily responsible for HBSS- and DMEMAcidic-driven MondoA transcriptional activity.
source: This slightly alkaline pH blocked TXNIP induction regardless of sodium bicarbonate concentration. (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), confirming that low pH rather than low sodium bicarbonate is primarily responsible for HBSS- and DMEMAcidic-driven MondoA transcriptional activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C showing pH clamping at 7.4 blocks TXNIP induction regardless of sodium bicarbonate concentration

claim: Acidosis drives MondoA nuclear accumulation, promoter binding and transcriptional activity.
source: Together these data establish that acidosis drives MondoA nuclear accumulation, promoter binding and transcriptional activity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments including luciferase reporter assays, ChIP, and complementation studies

claim: TXNIP induction in response to DMEMAcidic requires MondoA.
source: Consistent with this, TXNIP was induced in HeLa cells treated with DMEMAcidic but not in HeLa cells where we used CRISPR/Cas9 editing to disrupt MondoA expression (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 1D comparing HeLa and HeLa:MondoA-KO cells

claim: HBSS fails to increase TXNIP expression in MondoA-/- MEFs.
source: Likewise, HBSS failed to increase TXNIP expression in MondoA-/- MEFs but reconstituting MondoA null MEFs with human MondoA rescued TXNIP induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A

claim: Reconstituting MondoA null MEFs with human MondoA rescues TXNIP induction in response to HBSS.
source: Likewise, HBSS failed to increase TXNIP expression in MondoA-/- MEFs but reconstituting MondoA null MEFs with human MondoA rescued TXNIP induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A

claim: DMEMAcidic induces TXNIP expression in HeLa, HepG2 and 293T cells.
source: DMEMAcidic induced TXNIP expression in cell lines of different lineages: HeLa, HepG2 and 293 T cells (Figure 1E), indicating a conserved regulatory mechanism.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 1E

claim: The mechanism by which acidosis induces TXNIP expression is conserved across different cell lineages.
source: DMEMAcidic induced TXNIP expression in cell lines of different lineages: HeLa, HepG2 and 293 T cells (Figure 1E), indicating a conserved regulatory mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that DMEMAcidic induces TXNIP in multiple cell types

claim: MondoA(I766P) does not interact with Mlx.
source: MondoA(I766P), which does not interact with Mlx (Stoltzman et al., 2008), did not rescue TXNIP induction in MondoA null MEFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), which is consistent with several previous findings showing that MondoA requires Mlx as an obligate partner (Stoltzman et al., 2011; Peterson et al., 2010; Minn et al., 2005; Stoltzman et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from previous publication (Stoltzman et al., 2008)

claim: MondoA(I766P) does not rescue TXNIP induction in MondoA null MEFs.
source: MondoA(I766P), which does not interact with Mlx (Stoltzman et al., 2008), did not rescue TXNIP induction in MondoA null MEFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), which is consistent with several previous findings showing that MondoA requires Mlx as an obligate partner (Stoltzman et al., 2011; Peterson et al., 2010; Minn et al., 2005; Stoltzman et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A

claim: MondoA requires Mlx as an obligate partner.
source: MondoA(I766P), which does not interact with Mlx (Stoltzman et al., 2008), did not rescue TXNIP induction in MondoA null MEFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), which is consistent with several previous findings showing that MondoA requires Mlx as an obligate partner (Stoltzman et al., 2011; Peterson et al., 2010; Minn et al., 2005; Stoltzman et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from multiple previous publications (Stoltzman et al., 2011; Peterson et al., 2010; Minn et al., 2005; Stoltzman et al., 2008)

claim: HBSS induces activity from a TXNIP-promoter luciferase reporter.
source: HBSS also induced the activity from a TXNIP-promoter luciferase reporter, but not when the MondoA:Mlx Carbohydrate Response Element (ChoRE) binding site sequence was mutated (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C

claim: HBSS does not induce activity from a TXNIP-promoter luciferase reporter when the MondoA:Mlx ChoRE binding site is mutated.
source: HBSS also induced the activity from a TXNIP-promoter luciferase reporter, but not when the MondoA:Mlx Carbohydrate Response Element (ChoRE) binding site sequence was mutated (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C

claim: HBSS treatment increases MondoA occupancy at the TXNIP promoter.
source: Finally, HBSS treatment led to increased MondoA occupancy at the TXNIP promoter (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D

claim: Low pH growth medium drives intracellular acidification.
source: Previous reports show that low pH growth medium drives intracellular acidification (Adams et al., 2006; Wahl et al., 2000).
evidence: Cited from previous publications (Adams et al., 2006; Wahl et al., 2000)

claim: Monensin completely blocks HBSS-induced TXNIP expression.
source: Monensin, and the mitochondrial ionophore FCCP, which drive cytosolic alkalization and dissipation of the mitochondrial proton gradient, respectively, completely block HBSS-induced TXNIP expression (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2A

claim: FCCP completely blocks HBSS-induced TXNIP expression.
source: Monensin, and the mitochondrial ionophore FCCP, which drive cytosolic alkalization and dissipation of the mitochondrial proton gradient, respectively, completely block HBSS-induced TXNIP expression (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2B

claim: Monensin drives cytosolic alkalization.
source: Monensin, and the mitochondrial ionophore FCCP, which drive cytosolic alkalization and dissipation of the mitochondrial proton gradient, respectively, completely block HBSS-induced TXNIP expression (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Statement about the known mechanism of action of monensin

claim: FCCP dissipates the mitochondrial proton gradient.
source: Monensin, and the mitochondrial ionophore FCCP, which drive cytosolic alkalization and dissipation of the mitochondrial proton gradient, respectively, completely block HBSS-induced TXNIP expression (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Statement about the known mechanism of action of FCCP

claim: Chloroquine has no effect on HBSS-induced TXNIP expression.
source: By contrast, chloroquine, which disrupts acidification of endosomes/lysosomes, had no effect on TXNIP induction (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2A

claim: Chloroquine disrupts acidification of endosomes/lysosomes.
source: By contrast, chloroquine, which disrupts acidification of endosomes/lysosomes, had no effect on TXNIP induction (Figure 2A).
evidence: Statement about the known mechanism of action of chloroquine

claim: Cytosolic and/or mitochondrial proton gradients are critical for the activation of the MondoA/TXNIP axis.
source: Together these results suggest that cytosolic and/or mitochondrial proton gradients, but not pH-dependent changes in the endosome/lysosome, are critical for the activation of the MondoA/TXNIP axis.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of monensin, FCCP, and chloroquine on TXNIP induction

claim: pH-dependent changes in the endosome/lysosome are not critical for the activation of the MondoA/TXNIP axis.
source: Together these results suggest that cytosolic and/or mitochondrial proton gradients, but not pH-dependent changes in the endosome/lysosome, are critical for the activation of the MondoA/TXNIP axis.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of chloroquine on TXNIP induction

claim: MondoA requires a functional ETC for transcriptional activity.
source: Cytosolic and mitochondrial protons contribute to ETC activity and previous inhibitor studies demonstrate that MondoA requires a functional ETC for transcriptional activity (Yu et al., 2010; Han and Ayer, 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous publications (Yu et al., 2010; Han and Ayer, 2013)

claim: 143Bρ0 cells lack mitochondrial DNA and are respiration deficient.
source: We used 143Bρ0 osteosarcoma cells, which lack mitochondrial DNA and are respiration deficient (King and Attardi, 1989).
evidence: Cited from previous publication (King and Attardi, 1989)

claim: TXNIP is induced in parental 143B cells treated with DMEMAcidic.
source: TXNIP was induced in parental 143B cells treated with DMEMAcidic (Figure 2C), yet induction was blunted in 143Bρ0 cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2C

claim: TXNIP induction in response to DMEMAcidic is blunted in 143Bρ0 cells.
source: TXNIP was induced in parental 143B cells treated with DMEMAcidic (Figure 2C), yet induction was blunted in 143Bρ0 cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2D

claim: TXNIP induction is rescued in 143Bρ0 cells that had been repopulated with wild type mitochondria.
source: TXNIP induction was rescued in 143Bρ0 cells that had been repopulated with wild type mitochondria (143Bρ0:WT-cybrid cells; Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2E

claim: Metformin does not block TXNIP induction in response to DMEMAcidic.
source: Surprisingly, treatment of cells with the ETC complex I inhibitor metformin did not block TXNIP induction in response to DMEMAcidic suggesting that the ETC requirement may be downstream of complex I (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2B

claim: The ETC requirement for MondoA activity may be downstream of complex I.
source: Surprisingly, treatment of cells with the ETC complex I inhibitor metformin did not block TXNIP induction in response to DMEMAcidic suggesting that the ETC requirement may be downstream of complex I (Figure 2B).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that metformin does not block TXNIP induction

claim: 143Bρ0:ΔATP6/ΔATP8 cybrid cells have a point mutation in mtDNA that disrupts expression of both ATP6 and ATP8.
source: We used 143Bρ0:ΔATP6/ΔATP8 cybrid cells. These cells have a point mutation in mtDNA that disrupts expression of both ATP6 and ATP8, which are required components of the F0F1-ATPase (ATP synthase, Figure 2F) and consequently synthesize less mitochondrial ATP (Boominathan et al., 2016; Jonckheere et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from previous publications (Boominathan et al., 2016; Jonckheere et al., 2008)

claim: ATP6 and ATP8 are required components of the F0F1-ATPase (ATP synthase).
source: We used 143Bρ0:ΔATP6/ΔATP8 cybrid cells. These cells have a point mutation in mtDNA that disrupts expression of both ATP6 and ATP8, which are required components of the F0F1-ATPase (ATP synthase, Figure 2F) and consequently synthesize less mitochondrial ATP (Boominathan et al., 2016; Jonckheere et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from previous publications (Boominathan et al., 2016; Jonckheere et al., 2008) and illustrated in Figure 2F

claim: 143Bρ0:ΔATP6/ΔATP8 cybrid cells synthesize less mitochondrial ATP.
source: We used 143Bρ0:ΔATP6/ΔATP8 cybrid cells. These cells have a point mutation in mtDNA that disrupts expression of both ATP6 and ATP8, which are required components of the F0F1-ATPase (ATP synthase, Figure 2F) and consequently synthesize less mitochondrial ATP (Boominathan et al., 2016; Jonckheere et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from previous publications (Boominathan et al., 2016; Jonckheere et al., 2008)

claim: Low pH-driven TXNIP expression is reduced in 143Bρ0:ΔATP6/ΔATP8 cybrid cells.
source: Low pH-driven TXNIP expression was reduced in these cells, yet was partially rescued by expression of nuclear-encoded, but mitochondrially-targeted ATP6 and ATP8 (Figure 2G) (Boominathan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2G

claim: Expression of nuclear-encoded, but mitochondrially-targeted ATP6 and ATP8 partially rescues TXNIP expression in 143Bρ0:ΔATP6/ΔATP8 cybrid cells.
source: Low pH-driven TXNIP expression was reduced in these cells, yet was partially rescued by expression of nuclear-encoded, but mitochondrially-targeted ATP6 and ATP8 (Figure 2G) (Boominathan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2G

claim: mtATP synthesis is necessary for low pH to induce MondoA transcriptional activity.
source: These results suggest that mtATP synthesis is necessary for low pH to induce MondoA transcriptional activity.
evidence: Inferred from genetic experiments with 143Bρ0:ΔATP6/ΔATP8 cybrid cells

claim: Oligomycin completely blocks TXNIP induction in response to DMEMAcidic.
source: Complementing these two genetic experiments, the ATP synthase inhibitor oligomycin completely blocked TXNIP induction in response to DMEMAcidic (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2B

claim: Acidosis increases MondoA transcriptional activity by driving mtATP synthesis.
source: The experiments above suggest a critical role for mtATP in driving MondoA transcriptional activity and raise the possibility that acidosis increases MondoA transcriptional activity by driving mtATP synthesis.
evidence: Inferred from the genetic and pharmacological experiments showing requirement for ATP synthase

claim: The outer mitochondrial membrane is freely permeable to protons.
source: Because the outer mitochondrial membrane is freely permeable to protons (Cooper, 2000), we hypothesized that acidosis generates an ectopic proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane and the mitochondrial matrix that subsequently drives mtATP synthesis.
evidence: Cited from previous publication (Cooper, 2000)

claim: Acidosis generates an ectopic proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane and the mitochondrial matrix that subsequently drives mtATP synthesis.
source: Because the outer mitochondrial membrane is freely permeable to protons (Cooper, 2000), we hypothesized that acidosis generates an ectopic proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane and the mitochondrial matrix that subsequently drives mtATP synthesis.
evidence: Hypothesis based on the known permeability of the outer mitochondrial membrane to protons

claim: DMEMAcidic treatment shifts intracellular pH from 7.2 to 6.5.
source: First, DMEMAcidic treatment shifted intracellular pH from 7.2 to 6.5 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by BCECF-AM staining data in Figure 3A

claim: The drop in intracellular pH caused by DMEMAcidic is accompanied by an increase in mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Second, the drop in intracellular pH was accompanied by an increase in mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by JC1 staining data in Figure 3B

claim: DMEMAcidic treatment increases total cellular ATP levels.
source: Third, DMEMAcidic treatment increased in total cellular ATP levels (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by luciferase-based ATP assay data in Figure 3C

claim: Treating cells with low pH medium increases total cellular ATP levels.
source: Thus, treating cells with low pH medium increases total cellular ATP levels.
evidence: Conclusion from the ATP measurement experiment

claim: Acidic medium can suppress mTORC1 activity.
source: Others have shown that acidic medium can suppress mTORC1 activity (Walton et al., 2018), which under some circumstances can result in an ~10% increase in total ATP that stems from a blockade of mTORC1-dependent translation (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous publications (Walton et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2016)

claim: Blockade of mTORC1-dependent translation can result in an ~10% increase in total ATP.
source: Others have shown that acidic medium can suppress mTORC1 activity (Walton et al., 2018), which under some circumstances can result in an ~10% increase in total ATP that stems from a blockade of mTORC1-dependent translation (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous publication (Zheng et al., 2016)

claim: Extended time course of DMEMAcidic treatment does not result in significant suppression of mTORC1 activity.
source: However, even with an extend time course of DMEMAcidic treatment, we did not observe significant suppression of mTORC1 activity as assayed by levels of phosphorylated-S6 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: DMEMAcidic increases TXNIP expression by a mechanism that is largely independent of mTORC1 and its control of ATP pools.
source: This finding suggests that DMEMAcidic increases TXNIP expression by a mechanism that is largely independent of mTORC1 and its control of ATP pools.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of mTORC1 suppression by DMEMAcidic

claim: Metabolite levels in whole cell lysates can be vastly different from those observed in specific organelles.
source: DMEMAcidic increased total cellular ATP content (Figure 3C), however, metabolite levels in whole cell lysates can be vastly different from those observed in specific organelles (Abu-Remaileh et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous publications (Abu-Remaileh et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2016)

claim: Mit-ATEAM is targeted to the inner-mitochondrial matrix and measures mtATP pools.
source: ATEAM measures cytoplasmic ATP pools, whereas Mit-ATEAM, which is targeted to the inner-mitochondrial matrix, measures mtATP pools (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Description of the Mit-ATEAM biosensor tool, based on published methods (Imamura et al., 2009)

claim: ATEAM measures cytoplasmic ATP pools.
source: ATEAM measures cytoplasmic ATP pools, whereas Mit-ATEAM, which is targeted to the inner-mitochondrial matrix, measures mtATP pools (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Description of the ATEAM biosensor tool, based on published methods (Imamura et al., 2009)

claim: HeLa cells treated with DMEMAcidic show increased FRET from Mit-ATEAM.
source: HeLa cells treated with DMEMAcidic showed increased FRET from Mit-ATEAM but not from ATEAM indicating that acidosis drives an increase in mtATP but not in cytosolic ATP (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-E

claim: HeLa cells treated with DMEMAcidic do not show increased FRET from ATEAM.
source: HeLa cells treated with DMEMAcidic showed increased FRET from Mit-ATEAM but not from ATEAM indicating that acidosis drives an increase in mtATP but not in cytosolic ATP (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-E

claim: Acidosis drives an increase in mtATP but not in cytosolic ATP.
source: HeLa cells treated with DMEMAcidic showed increased FRET from Mit-ATEAM but not from ATEAM indicating that acidosis drives an increase in mtATP but not in cytosolic ATP (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: Inferred from the differential FRET signals from Mit-ATEAM and ATEAM

claim: DMEMAcidic treatment increases total cellular ATP levels primarily by increasing mtATP synthesis.
source: DMEMAcidic treatment increased total ATP pools, yet we only observed an increase in mtATP and not in cytosolic ATP in this assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and E). This finding suggests that DMEMAcidic treatment increases total cellular ATP levels primarily by increasing mtATP synthesis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that total ATP increases but only mtATP (not cytosolic ATP) increases

claim: ATP5I knockdown decreases the steady state level of mtATP.
source: Consistent with our working model, ATP5I knockdown not only decreased the steady state level of mtATP, but also the DMEMAcidic-driven increase in mtATP (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by Mit-ATEAM imaging data in Figure 3F

claim: ATP5I knockdown decreases the DMEMAcidic-driven increase in mtATP.
source: Consistent with our working model, ATP5I knockdown not only decreased the steady state level of mtATP, but also the DMEMAcidic-driven increase in mtATP (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by Mit-ATEAM imaging data in Figure 3F

claim: ATP5I knockdown prevents TXNIP induction in response to DMEMAcidic treatment.
source: Furthermore, ATP5I knockdown prevented TXNIP induction in response to DMEMAcidic treatment (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 3G

claim: Low pH medium drives mtATP production through ATP synthase.
source: Together these data suggest that low pH medium drives mtATP production through ATP synthase and that mtATP synthesis is required for DMEMAcidic to drive MondoA transcriptional activity.
evidence: Conclusion from ATP5I knockdown experiments

claim: mtATP synthesis is required for DMEMAcidic to drive MondoA transcriptional activity.
source: Together these data suggest that low pH medium drives mtATP production through ATP synthase and that mtATP synthesis is required for DMEMAcidic to drive MondoA transcriptional activity.
evidence: Conclusion from ATP5I knockdown experiments showing both reduced mtATP and reduced TXNIP induction

claim: MondoA, Mlx and hexokinase 2 (HK2) are all resident at the outer mitochondrial membrane.
source: MondoA, Mlx and hexokinase 2 (HK2) are all resident at the outer mitochondrial membrane (Figure 4A–B) (Robey and Hay, 2006; Sans et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by cellular fractionation data in Figure 4A and cited from previous publications (Robey and Hay, 2006; Sans et al., 2006)

claim: Mitochondria-bound HK2 has preferential access to mtATP as it is exported from the mitochondria.
source: Mitochondria-bound HK2 has preferential access to mtATP as it is exported from the mitochondria (Wilson, 2003) and it transfers the terminal phosphate from ATP to cytoplasmic glucose to generate G6P.
evidence: Cited from previous publication (Wilson, 2003)

claim: Mitochondria-bound HK2 transfers the terminal phosphate from ATP to cytoplasmic glucose to generate G6P.
source: Mitochondria-bound HK2 has preferential access to mtATP as it is exported from the mitochondria (Wilson, 2003) and it transfers the terminal phosphate from ATP to cytoplasmic glucose to generate G6P.
evidence: Statement about the enzymatic function of hexokinase

claim: G6P is a known activator of MondoA transcriptional activity.
source: Because G6P is a known activator of MondoA transcriptional activity, we speculated that DMEMAcidic-induced mtATP synthesis drives G6P synthesis resulting in a stimulation of MondoA transcriptional activity (Figure 4B).
evidence: Referenced as established knowledge from previous work

claim: DMEMAcidic-induced mtATP synthesis drives G6P synthesis resulting in a stimulation of MondoA transcriptional activity.
source: Because G6P is a known activator of MondoA transcriptional activity, we speculated that DMEMAcidic-induced mtATP synthesis drives G6P synthesis resulting in a stimulation of MondoA transcriptional activity (Figure 4B).
evidence: Hypothesis based on the known role of G6P in MondoA activation and the observed increase in mtATP

claim: Acidosis leads to increased mitochondrial metabolism.
source: Consistent with reports showing that acidosis leads to increased mitochondrial metabolism (Lamonte et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2008; Dietl et al., 2010), DMEMAcidic drove an increase in TCA cycle intermediates (Figure 4C).
evidence: Cited from previous publications (Lamonte et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2008; Dietl et al., 2010)

claim: DMEMAcidic drives an increase in TCA cycle intermediates.
source: Consistent with reports showing that acidosis leads to increased mitochondrial metabolism (Lamonte et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2008; Dietl et al., 2010), DMEMAcidic drove an increase in TCA cycle intermediates (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS metabolomics data in Figure 4C

claim: Most glycolytic intermediates are decreased in response to DMEMAcidic.
source: Most glycolytic intermediates were decreased in response to DMEMAcidic; however, G6P levels increased 3-fold (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS metabolomics data in Figure 4C

claim: G6P levels increase 3-fold in response to DMEMAcidic.
source: Most glycolytic intermediates were decreased in response to DMEMAcidic; however, G6P levels increased 3-fold (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS metabolomics data in Figure 4C

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of ANT2 prevents TXNIP induction in response to low pH medium.
source: Consistent with our working model, which states that mtATP must be exported from the matrix to drive MondoA transcriptional activity, siRNA-mediated knockdown of ANT2 prevented TXNIP induction in response to low pH medium (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 4D

claim: mtATP functions outside the mitochondria to trigger MondoA transcriptional activity, rather than by an indirect signaling-based mechanism.
source: This finding suggests that mtATP functions outside the mitochondria to trigger MondoA transcriptional activity, rather than by an indirect signaling-based mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement for ANT2, which exports ATP from mitochondria

claim: siRNA pools against HK2 block TXNIP induction in response to low pH treatment.
source: Consistent with our previous reports (Stoltzman et al., 2008), siRNA pools against HK2 blocked TXNIP induction in response to low pH treatment (Figure 4E), demonstrating a requirement for HK2.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 4E

claim: HK2 is required for TXNIP induction in response to low pH treatment.
source: Consistent with our previous reports (Stoltzman et al., 2008), siRNA pools against HK2 blocked TXNIP induction in response to low pH treatment (Figure 4E), demonstrating a requirement for HK2.
evidence: Inferred from the siRNA knockdown experiment

claim: Overexpression of HK2(D657A), which lacks enzymatic activity, blocks the induction of TXNIP in response to DMEMAcidic.
source: Further, overexpression of HK2(D657A), which lacks emzymatic activity (Arora et al., 1991), blocked the induction of TXNIP in response to DMEMAcidic (Figure 4F), supporting the notion that HK2 activity and the formation of G6P is critical for the induction of MondoA transcriptional activity.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 4F

claim: HK2(D657A) lacks enzymatic activity.
source: Further, overexpression of HK2(D657A), which lacks emzymatic activity (Arora et al., 1991), blocked the induction of TXNIP in response to DMEMAcidic (Figure 4F), supporting the notion that HK2 activity and the formation of G6P is critical for the induction of MondoA transcriptional activity.
evidence: Cited from previous publication (Arora et al., 1991)

claim: HK2 activity and the formation of G6P is critical for the induction of MondoA transcriptional activity.
source: Further, overexpression of HK2(D657A), which lacks emzymatic activity (Arora et al., 1991), blocked the induction of TXNIP in response to DMEMAcidic (Figure 4F), supporting the notion that HK2 activity and the formation of G6P is critical for the induction of MondoA transcriptional activity.
evidence: Inferred from the dominant-negative effect of catalytically inactive HK2

claim: HK2 localizes to the outer-mitochondrial membrane via interactions with VDAC.
source: HK2 localizes to the outer-mitochondrial membrane via interactions with VDAC (Wilson, 2003).
evidence: Cited from previous publication (Wilson, 2003)

claim: mVDAC(E72Q) prevents the interaction between VDAC and HK2.
source: Ectopic expression of mVDAC(E72Q), a mutant of the mouse orthologue of VDAC1, which prevents the interaction between VDAC and HK2 (Abu-Hamad et al., 2008; Zaid et al., 2005), blocked the mitochondrial localization of HK2 as expected and completely blocked TXNIP induction in response to DMEMAcidic (Figure 5A).
evidence: Cited from previous publications (Abu-Hamad et al., 2008; Zaid et al., 2005)

claim: Ectopic expression of mVDAC(E72Q) blocks the mitochondrial localization of HK2.
source: Ectopic expression of mVDAC(E72Q), a mutant of the mouse orthologue of VDAC1, which prevents the interaction between VDAC and HK2 (Abu-Hamad et al., 2008; Zaid et al., 2005), blocked the mitochondrial localization of HK2 as expected and completely blocked TXNIP induction in response to DMEMAcidic (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by cellular fractionation data in Figure 5A

claim: Ectopic expression of mVDAC(E72Q) completely blocks TXNIP induction in response to DMEMAcidic.
source: Ectopic expression of mVDAC(E72Q), a mutant of the mouse orthologue of VDAC1, which prevents the interaction between VDAC and HK2 (Abu-Hamad et al., 2008; Zaid et al., 2005), blocked the mitochondrial localization of HK2 as expected and completely blocked TXNIP induction in response to DMEMAcidic (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 5A

claim: Expression of mVDAC1(E72Q)-GFP(1-10) blocks TXNIP induction.
source: Expression of mVDAC1(E72Q)-GFP(1-10), which does not interact with HK2, blocked TXNIP induction (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 5C

claim: Co-expression of mVDAC1(E72Q)-GFP(1-10) and HK2-GFP(11) rescues HK2 mitochondrial localization.
source: However, co-expression of mVDAC1(E72Q)-GFP(1-10) and HK2-GFP(11) rescued HK2 mitochondrial localization and TXNIP induction (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: Supported by cellular fractionation data in Figure 5B

claim: Co-expression of mVDAC1(E72Q)-GFP(1-10) and HK2-GFP(11) rescues TXNIP induction.
source: However, co-expression of mVDAC1(E72Q)-GFP(1-10) and HK2-GFP(11) rescued HK2 mitochondrial localization and TXNIP induction (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 5C

claim: Mitochondrial-localized HK2 is both necessary and sufficient for low pH medium to drive MondoA activity.
source: Together these data show that mitochondrial-localized HK2 is both necessary and sufficient for low pH medium to drive MondoA activity.
evidence: Conclusion from loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments with VDAC mutants and GFP complementation

claim: DMEMAcidic treatment drives an increase in MondoA nuclear localization in cells treated with an siRNA control.
source: While the majority of MondoA resides in the cytosol (Figure 5D), DMEMAcidic treatment drove an increase in MondoA nuclear localization in cells treated with an siRNA control (Figure 5D); however, MondoA nuclear accumulation was blunted in cells treated with siRNA pools against ATP5I, ANT2 or HK2 (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by cellular fractionation data in Figure 5D

claim: MondoA nuclear accumulation is blunted in cells treated with siRNA pools against ATP5I, ANT2 or HK2.
source: While the majority of MondoA resides in the cytosol (Figure 5D), DMEMAcidic treatment drove an increase in MondoA nuclear localization in cells treated with an siRNA control (Figure 5D); however, MondoA nuclear accumulation was blunted in cells treated with siRNA pools against ATP5I, ANT2 or HK2 (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by cellular fractionation data in Figure 5D

claim: mtATP synthesis and the subsequent production of G6P by OMM-bound HK2 drive MondoA nuclear accumulation, occupation of the TXNIP promoter and activation of TXNIP transcription in response to low pH medium.
source: In combination with the above experiments, these findings suggest that mtATP synthesis and the subsequent production of G6P by OMM-bound HK2 drive MondoA nuclear accumulation, occupation of the TXNIP promoter and activation of TXNIP transcription in response to low pH medium.
evidence: Conclusion from the series of experiments showing requirements for ATP5I, ANT2, and HK2 in MondoA nuclear localization

claim: 617 genes are differentially regulated in HeLa cells treated with DMEMAcidic (using a 1.5-fold cut off and an adjusted p-value of ≤0.01).
source: Using a 1.5-fold cut off and an adjusted p-value of ≤0.01, we identified 617 differentially regulated genes in HeLa cells treated with DMEMAcidic.
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing analysis

claim: 227 of the 617 acidosis-regulated genes are not regulated in HeLa:MondoA-KO cells.
source: Of these, 227 were not regulated in HeLa:MondoA-KO cells, suggesting that MondoA contributes to nearly 37% of the acidosis-driven transcriptional response.
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing analysis comparing HeLa and HeLa:MondoA-KO cells

claim: MondoA contributes to nearly 37% of the acidosis-driven transcriptional response.
source: Of these, 227 were not regulated in HeLa:MondoA-KO cells, suggesting that MondoA contributes to nearly 37% of the acidosis-driven transcriptional response.
evidence: Calculated from RNA-sequencing data (227/617 = ~37%)

claim: The expression of only two genes, TXNIP and ARRDC4, are entirely dependent on MondoA following DMEMAcidic treatment.
source: Loss of MondoA prevented the induction/suppression of several acidosis-regulated genes; however, the expression only two genes, TXNIP and one of its paralogues, ARRDC4, were entirely dependent on MondoA (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: ARRDC4 is a paralogue of TXNIP.
source: Loss of MondoA prevented the induction/suppression of several acidosis-regulated genes; however, the expression only two genes, TXNIP and one of its paralogues, ARRDC4, were entirely dependent on MondoA (Figure 6A).
evidence: Statement about the relationship between TXNIP and ARRDC4

claim: TXNIP and ARRDC4 are the most highly MondoA-dependent genes, with log2(fold-change) decrease of 7.9 and 5.1, respectively.
source: Consistent with the results above, TXNIP and ARRDC4 were the most highly MondoA-dependent genes, with log2(fold-change) decrease of 7.9 and 5.1, respectively (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: Pathways that are upregulated in HeLa:MondoA-KO cells are enriched for fatty acid metabolism, sterol biosynthesis, ion homeostasis, ROS metabolism, and pyridine metabolism pathways.
source: Pathways that were upregulated in HeLa:MondoA-KO cells were enriched for fatty acid metabolism, sterol biosynthesis, ion homeostasis, ROS metabolism, and pyridine metabolism pathways, whereas cell death and proliferation pathways were downregulated (Figure 6B, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: Cell death and proliferation pathways are downregulated in HeLa:MondoA-KO cells.
source: Pathways that were upregulated in HeLa:MondoA-KO cells were enriched for fatty acid metabolism, sterol biosynthesis, ion homeostasis, ROS metabolism, and pyridine metabolism pathways, whereas cell death and proliferation pathways were downregulated (Figure 6B, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: Leading-edge analysis highlighted extracellular matrix remodeling, electron transport chain and ion transport as upregulated in HeLa:MondoA-KO cells.
source: Leading-edge analysis highlighted extracellular matrix remodeling, electron transport chain and ion transport as upregulated, and growth-factor/proliferation as downregulated in HeLa:MondoA-KO cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by GSEA and leading-edge analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: Growth-factor/proliferation pathways are downregulated in HeLa:MondoA-KO cells.
source: Leading-edge analysis highlighted extracellular matrix remodeling, electron transport chain and ion transport as upregulated, and growth-factor/proliferation as downregulated in HeLa:MondoA-KO cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by GSEA and leading-edge analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: MondoA is required for the transcriptional response to DMEMAcidic treatment.
source: Together these data show that MondoA is required for the transcriptional response to DMEMAcidic treatment and suggests that MondoA may have an essential role in an adaptive transcriptional response to acidosis.
evidence: Conclusion from RNA-sequencing analysis showing MondoA-dependent gene expression changes

claim: MondoA may have an essential role in an adaptive transcriptional response to acidosis.
source: Together these data show that MondoA is required for the transcriptional response to DMEMAcidic treatment and suggests that MondoA may have an essential role in an adaptive transcriptional response to acidosis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that MondoA is required for a large portion of the acidosis-driven transcriptional response

claim: MondoA occupies ~700 sites in normal pH media.
source: MondoA occupied ~700 sites in normal pH media and the occupancy of these sites increased following DMEMAcidic treatment.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq analysis

claim: The occupancy of MondoA binding sites increases following DMEMAcidic treatment.
source: MondoA occupied ~700 sites in normal pH media and the occupancy of these sites increased following DMEMAcidic treatment.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq analysis

claim: 128 of the ~700 MondoA binding sites are located within ±2000 base pairs of the transcriptional start site of the nearest gene.
source: Of these 700 sites, 128 were located within ±2000 base pairs of the transcriptional start site of the nearest gene (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 7A

claim: The binding sites in the promoters of TXNIP and ARRDC4 display much higher MondoA occupancy compared to its occupancy of other promoter binding sites.
source: The binding sites in the promoters of TXNIP and ARRDC4 displayed much higher MondoA occupancy compared to its occupancy of other promoter binding sites (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 7B and C

claim: The amount of MondoA on the TXNIP promoter is about twice that observed on the ARRDC4 promoter.
source: Relative to the input controls, the amount of MondoA on the TXNIP promoter was about twice that observed on the ARRDC4 promoter.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-PCR validation

claim: Occupancy of MondoA on the KLF10 promoter is reduced approximately 30-fold relative to the TXNIP promoter.
source: Relative to the high occupancy of MondoA on the TXNIP promoter, occupancy of MondoA on the KLF10 and TMEM97 promoters was reduced approximately 30 and 60 fold (Figure 7D), respectively.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-PCR data in Figure 7D

claim: Occupancy of MondoA on the TMEM97 promoter is reduced approximately 60-fold relative to the TXNIP promoter.
source: Relative to the high occupancy of MondoA on the TXNIP promoter, occupancy of MondoA on the KLF10 and TMEM97 promoters was reduced approximately 30 and 60 fold (Figure 7D), respectively.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-PCR data in Figure 7D

claim: The magnitude of increase in MondoA occupancy at all targets following DMEMAcidic treatment is within a fairly narrow range.
source: Regardless of the amount of MondoA bound at a given promoter in DMEM, the magnitude of increase at all targets following DMEMAcidic treatment was within a fairly narrow range (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: The ETC signal required for MondoA transcriptional activity is mtATP.
source: Previous studies established that MondoA's transcriptional activity is highly-dependent on two signals: glucose and a signal from the ETC. By dissecting how low pH drives MondoA transcriptional activity, we establish that the ETC signal is mtATP.
evidence: Conclusion from the series of experiments showing requirement for ATP synthase and mtATP production

claim: mtATP is a general requirement for MondoA transcriptional activity.
source: Previous studies showed that a functional ETC is required for basal TXNIP expression, thus we propose that mtATP is a general requirement for MondoA transcriptional activity.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement for mtATP in acidosis-driven MondoA activity and previous findings about ETC requirement

claim: Via the activity of OMM-bound HK2, mtATP couples to cytoplasmic glucose to generate G6P, which drives the nuclear accumulation and transcriptional activity of MondoA:Mlx complexes.
source: Via the activity of OMM-bound HK2, mtATP couples to cytoplasmic glucose to generate G6P, which drives the nuclear accumulation and transcriptional activity of MondoA:Mlx complexes (Figure 8).
evidence: Summary of the mechanistic model supported by the experimental data

claim: MondoA:Mlx and HK2 constitute a sensing and response module that integrates signals from the cytoplasm and the mitochondria to coordinate the transcriptional response to the cell's two predominant energy sources.
source: Therefore, we propose that MondoA:Mlx and HK2 constitute a sensing and response module that integrates signals from the cytoplasm and the mitochondria to coordinate the transcriptional response to the cell's two predominant energy sources.
evidence: Proposed model based on the OMM localization of MondoA, Mlx, and HK2 and their functional interactions

claim: MondoA may be activated by a pH-dependent mechanism that is independent of functional mitochondria.
source: MondoA also appears to be activated by pH-dependent mechanism that is independent of functional mitochondria (Figure 2B and G).
evidence: Inferred from the partial TXNIP induction observed in 143Bρ0 cells and with metformin treatment

claim: There are conserved histidines in MondoA Conserved Region 1 and in the DNA-binding basic region, which have titratable protons in the physiological range.
source: There are a number of conserved histidines, which have titratable protons in the physiological range, in MondoA Conserved Region 1 and in the DNA-binding basic region (McFerrin and Atchley, 2012), which may account for this effect.
evidence: Cited from previous publication (McFerrin and Atchley, 2012)

claim: By binding mitochondria, hexokinase has increased specific activity and decreased feedback inhibition by G6P.
source: By binding mitochondria, hexokinase has increased specific activity and decreased feedback inhibition by G6P (Robey and Hay, 2006).
evidence: Cited from previous publication (Robey and Hay, 2006)

claim: By localizing to the mitochondria and sensing G6P derived from mitochondria-bound hexokinase, MondoA activity is coupled to mitochondrial hexokinase activity and mtATP synthesis.
source: By localizing to the mitochondria and sensing G6P derived from mitochondria-bound hexokinase, we propose that MondoA activity is coupled to mitochondrial hexokinase activity and mtATP synthesis.
evidence: Proposed model based on the OMM localization and functional requirements

claim: The OMM serves as a scaffold for nutrient sensing by MondoA, akin to other nutrient sensors that are tethered to organellar membranes.
source: Given the OMM localization of MondoA, Mlx and HK2, we suggest that the OMM serves as a scaffold for nutrient sensing by MondoA, akin to other nutrient sensors that are tethered to organellar membranes.
evidence: Proposed model by analogy to other membrane-tethered nutrient sensors

claim: The mTORC1 complex is tethered to the lysosome where it integrates intra-lysosomal nutrient levels and cytosolic growth factor signals to control biosynthesis.
source: For example, the mTORC1 complex is tethered to the lysosome where it integrates intra-lysosomal nutrient levels and cytosolic growth factor signals to control biosynthesis (Wolfson and Sabatini, 2017), and the SREBP/Scap complex which is resident in the ER membrane where it monitors cholesterol and oxysterol availability and controls a transcriptional response to low sterol levels (Moon, 2017).
evidence: Cited from previous publication (Wolfson and Sabatini, 2017)

claim: The SREBP/Scap complex is resident in the ER membrane where it monitors cholesterol and oxysterol availability and controls a transcriptional response to low sterol levels.
source: For example, the mTORC1 complex is tethered to the lysosome where it integrates intra-lysosomal nutrient levels and cytosolic growth factor signals to control biosynthesis (Wolfson and Sabatini, 2017), and the SREBP/Scap complex which is resident in the ER membrane where it monitors cholesterol and oxysterol availability and controls a transcriptional response to low sterol levels (Moon, 2017).
evidence: Cited from previous publication (Moon, 2017)

claim: MondoA functions as a coincidence detector which simultaneously senses mtATP and glucose through the synthesis of G6P.
source: Our data suggest that MondoA functions as a coincidence detector which simultaneously senses mtATP and glucose through the synthesis of G6P (Figure 8).
evidence: Proposed model based on the requirement for both mtATP and glucose for MondoA activity

claim: By coupling mtATP and cytosolic glucose, MondoA functions as a sensor of high cellular energy charge.
source: Conceptually, by coupling mtATP and cytosolic glucose, MondoA functions as a sensor of high cellular energy charge and via its transcriptional regulation of TXNIP, ARRDC4 and potentially other targets, restricts glucose uptake and aerobic glycolysis to restore energy balance.
evidence: Proposed model based on the integration of mtATP and glucose signals

claim: Via its transcriptional regulation of TXNIP, ARRDC4 and potentially other targets, MondoA restricts glucose uptake and aerobic glycolysis to restore energy balance.
source: Conceptually, by coupling mtATP and cytosolic glucose, MondoA functions as a sensor of high cellular energy charge and via its transcriptional regulation of TXNIP, ARRDC4 and potentially other targets, restricts glucose uptake and aerobic glycolysis to restore energy balance.
evidence: Proposed model based on the known function of TXNIP in suppressing glucose uptake

claim: High TXNIP levels are correlated with oxidation of triglycerides, branched chain amino acids and lactate.
source: Further, high TXNIP levels are correlated with oxidation of triglycerides, branched chain amino acids and lactate (DeBalsi et al., 2014; Bodnar et al., 2002), suggesting an additional role for the MondoA/TXNIP axis in driving utilization of non-glucose fuels when cellular energy charge is high.
evidence: Cited from previous publications (DeBalsi et al., 2014; Bodnar et al., 2002)

claim: The MondoA/TXNIP axis may have an additional role in driving utilization of non-glucose fuels when cellular energy charge is high.
source: Further, high TXNIP levels are correlated with oxidation of triglycerides, branched chain amino acids and lactate (DeBalsi et al., 2014; Bodnar et al., 2002), suggesting an additional role for the MondoA/TXNIP axis in driving utilization of non-glucose fuels when cellular energy charge is high.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between TXNIP and oxidation of non-glucose fuels

claim: Changes in intracellular pH have dramatic effects on cell function: generally acidic pH is anti-proliferative whereas alkaline pH is pro-proliferative.
source: Changes in intracellular pH have dramatic effects on cell function: generally acidic pH is anti-proliferative whereas alkaline pH is pro-proliferative.
evidence: Statement about established knowledge of pH effects on cell function

claim: Acidic intercellular pH is correlated with an inhibition of aerobic glycolysis and a blockage of glucose uptake.
source: Acidic intercellular pH is correlated with an inhibition of aerobic glycolysis and a blockage of glucose uptake (Webb et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from previous publication (Webb et al., 2011)

claim: TXNIP induction contributes to the suppression of glucose metabolism driven by acidic pH.
source: Our data suggest that TXNIP induction contributes to this suppression of glucose metabolism driven by acidic pH.
evidence: Inferred from the observed TXNIP induction by acidic pH and the known role of TXNIP in suppressing glucose uptake

claim: An acidosis-dependent gene signature, of which TXNIP is a member, correlates with better clinical outcomes in breast cancer.
source: Further, an acidosis-dependent gene signature, of which TXNIP is a member correlates with better clinical outcomes in breast cancer (Chen et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from previous publications (Chen et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2008)

claim: Otto Warburg noted that increased sodium bicarbonate and alkaline pH favor glycolysis.
source: Interestingly, Otto Warburg noted that increased sodium bicarbonate and alkaline pH favor glycolysis (Koppenol et al., 2011; Warburg, 1925).
evidence: Cited from previous publications (Koppenol et al., 2011; Warburg, 1925)

claim: Intracellular alkalization is a widely accepted hallmark of cancer metabolism.
source: Intracellular alkalization is now a widely accepted hallmark of cancer metabolism (Webb et al., 2011), that has pleiotropic effects on tumorigenesis, the most predominant being a transition from oxidative metabolism to aerobic glycolysis (Reshkin et al., 2000).
evidence: Cited from previous publications (Webb et al., 2011; Reshkin et al., 2000)

claim: Intracellular alkalization has pleiotropic effects on tumorigenesis, the most predominant being a transition from oxidative metabolism to aerobic glycolysis.
source: Intracellular alkalization is now a widely accepted hallmark of cancer metabolism (Webb et al., 2011), that has pleiotropic effects on tumorigenesis, the most predominant being a transition from oxidative metabolism to aerobic glycolysis (Reshkin et al., 2000).
evidence: Cited from previous publication (Reshkin et al., 2000)

claim: MondoA transcriptional activity at the TXNIP promoter is suppressed by high sodium bicarbonate and alkaline pH.
source: Because, MondoA transcriptional activity at the TXNIP promoter is suppressed by high sodium bicarbonate and alkaline pH (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C), we propose that TXNIP down regulation contributes to the shift to high glucose uptake driven by alkaline pH.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C

claim: TXNIP down regulation contributes to the shift to high glucose uptake driven by alkaline pH.
source: Because, MondoA transcriptional activity at the TXNIP promoter is suppressed by high sodium bicarbonate and alkaline pH (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C), we propose that TXNIP down regulation contributes to the shift to high glucose uptake driven by alkaline pH.
evidence: Proposed model based on the suppression of TXNIP by alkaline pH

claim: MondoA is essential for the regulation of 37% of an acidosis-driven transcriptional response.
source: Our gene expression data demonstrates that MondoA is essential for the regulation of 37% of an acidosis-driven transcriptional response.
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing analysis

claim: Among the MondoA-dependent genes are fatty acid and mitochondrial metabolism genes.
source: Among the MondoA-dependent genes are fatty acid and mitochondrial metabolism genes.
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis of RNA-sequencing data

claim: Fatty acid and mitochondrial metabolism pathways are enhanced by acidosis.
source: Given that these pathways are enhanced by acidosis (Corbet et al., 2016; Lamonte et al., 2013; Khacho et al., 2014), we propose that MondoA plays a critical role in an adaptive metabolic response to acidosis.
evidence: Cited from previous publications (Corbet et al., 2016; Lamonte et al., 2013; Khacho et al., 2014)

claim: MondoA plays a critical role in an adaptive metabolic response to acidosis.
source: Given that these pathways are enhanced by acidosis (Corbet et al., 2016; Lamonte et al., 2013; Khacho et al., 2014), we propose that MondoA plays a critical role in an adaptive metabolic response to acidosis.
evidence: Inferred from the MondoA-dependence of fatty acid and mitochondrial metabolism genes that are enhanced by acidosis

claim: MondoA binds the TXNIP and ARRDC4 promoters at least an order of magnitude more strongly than other promoter binding sites.
source: Our ChIP-seq and ChIP-PCR analysis revealed the MondoA binds the TXNIP and ARRDC4 promoters at least an order of magnitude more strongly than other promoter binding sites.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and ChIP-PCR data

claim: The high occupancy of TXNIP and ARRDC4 promoters by MondoA likely accounts for their high MondoA-dependence at baseline and following DMEMAcidic treatment.
source: This likely accounts their high MondoA-dependence at baseline and following DMEMAcidic treatment.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between high MondoA occupancy and high MondoA-dependence

claim: An enrichment of high affinity E-boxes in the promoters of the TXNIP and ARRDC4 promoters is apparently not sufficient to account for their high occupancy by MondoA.
source: An enrichment of high affinity E-boxes in the promoters of the TXNIP and ARRDC4 promoters is apparently not sufficient to account for their high occupancy by MondoA (data not shown).
evidence: Statement about unpublished analysis

claim: Features outside the primary sequence of the binding site, such as chromatin modifications or ancillary chromatin-binding factors must contribute to high affinity MondoA binding.
source: The relative increase in MondoA occupancy following DMEMAcidic treatment is similar at all of its binding sites, further supporting the idea that features outside the primary sequence of the binding site, such as chromatin modifications or ancillary chromatin-binding factors must contribute to high affinity MondoA binding.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that E-box enrichment alone doesn't explain high occupancy

claim: TXNIP and ARRDC4 are the primary MondoA effectors in the cellular transcriptional response to low pH.
source: Together these data suggest that TXNIP and ARRDC4 are the primary MondoA effectors in the cellular transcriptional response to low pH.
evidence: Conclusion from RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data showing high MondoA-dependence and high MondoA occupancy

claim: Oncogenes drive a shift from oxidative metabolism to aerobic glycolysis.
source: Finally, it is well established that oncogenes drive a shift from oxidative metabolism to aerobic glycolysis (Pavlova and Thompson, 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous publication (Pavlova and Thompson, 2016)

claim: The shift away from ATP synthesis in the mitochondria to ATP synthesized by glycolysis in the cytosol would be predicted to restrict MondoA-dependent activation of TXNIP expression and reinforce glucose uptake and aerobic glycolysis.
source: The resulting shift away from ATP synthesis in the mitochondria to ATP synthesized by glycolysis in the cytosol would be predicted to restrict MondoA-dependent activation of TXNIP expression and reinforce glucose uptake and aerobic glycolysis.
evidence: Predicted consequence based on the established requirement for mtATP in MondoA activity

claim: TXNIP expression is downregulated by a variety of pro-growth signals such as mTOR, PI3K, Ras and Myc.
source: Strikingly, TXNIP expression is also downregulated by a variety of pro-growth signals such as mTOR, PI3K, Ras and Myc (Elgort et al., 2010; Kaadige et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2015), which results in increased glucose uptake.
evidence: Cited from previous publications (Elgort et al., 2010; Kaadige et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2015)

claim: Downregulation of TXNIP by pro-growth signals results in increased glucose uptake.
source: Strikingly, TXNIP expression is also downregulated by a variety of pro-growth signals such as mTOR, PI3K, Ras and Myc (Elgort et al., 2010; Kaadige et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2015), which results in increased glucose uptake.
evidence: Cited from previous publications (Elgort et al., 2010; Kaadige et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2015)

claim: MondoA and its regulation of TXNIP are both upstream and downstream of metabolic reprogramming towards aerobic glycolysis.
source: Together these two findings place MondoA and its regulation of TXNIP both upstream and downstream of metabolic reprogramming towards aerobic glycolysis.
evidence: Inferred from the dual observations that (1) reduced mtATP would restrict MondoA activity and (2) pro-growth signals downregulate TXNIP
